title: Automated Tortilla Machine Prototype
text:
Overview
I designed, analyzed, and fabricated an automated mechanical production system for making tortillas. The machine is driven by a DC worm gear motor that powers a waterjet-cut gear train, which in turn runs a set of integrated roller assemblies and a custom conveyor route for handling and processing dough.

title: Automated Tortilla Machine Prototype
text:
What I Built

Drive system: a DC worm gear motor feeding a gear train that I designed and cut on the waterjet.
Roller assemblies: integrated rollers that handle and mechanically process the dough.
Conveyor routing: a custom conveyor path that moves dough through the machine automatically.
Analysis and fabrication: the mechanism was analyzed in the design phase, then fabricated and assembled as a working prototype.

text:
Design Process
Everything started in SolidWorks, where I modeled the gear train, roller assemblies, and conveyor path together so the whole mechanism could be checked for fit and motion before cutting any material. Flat parts such as the gears were then cut on the waterjet.

title: Wearable IR Motion-Tracking Glove & Display Interface
text:
Overview
A wearable glove that turns hand motion into input. An STM32 microcontroller reads IR sensors on the glove to track spatial motion in real time, and the glove works as a wireless gesture controller. A custom display driver, written in SystemVerilog and running on an FPGA, renders an interactive UI and visual feedback so you can see your gestures respond.

title: Wearable IR Motion-Tracking Glove & Display Interface
text:
Goals

Track hand position and motion in real time using IR sensors read by an STM32.
Send gesture data wirelessly so the glove can control a separate display.
Build a high-speed SPI/UART link between the microcontroller and the FPGA.
Design a custom FPGA display driver that draws an interactive interface and gives visual feedback.

Lab 6: IoT, Web Server, and SPI
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated GitHub repository.

Schematic






Figure 1: Schematic of the physical circuit.



Figure 1 shows the physical layout of the design. The three main interactions are between the MCU and the ESP which share power and ground and are cross connected with TX and RX. Additionally, the design includes the DS1722 which is a digital temperature sensor we use via SPI.

title: Lab 6: IoT, Web Server, and SPI
text:
SPI Communication Logic Trace
When the SPI communication is working properly, we should see the following logic trace in the waveform viewer. The following screenshot shows the expected behavior of the SPI communication between the MCU and the DS1722 temperature sensor. It should be noted that the button that triggered this trace is the “9 bits” button on the web server and the reading on the server said 25 degrees Celsius.






Figure 2: Logic Trace of the SPI communication between the MCU and the DS1722 temperature sensor.



The top trace is the lsbRead function in my code, because looking at the MOSI sent (in blue) we see 0x01 which corresponds to the address byte for the LSB register. For MISO, we get FF which corresponds to floating high showing all high bits. For the second byte (pair of 8 bits) we get 00 on MOSI and 00 on MISO meaning a clock out. Basically, here we are querying the LSB register and reading 0x00 in the data byte.
In the middle transaction, MOSI sends 0x00, the address byte of the config register. MISO once again receives FF. The second byte is a dummy byte for MOSI (to clock in data from the DS1722) but MISO reads E2 which is exactly the decoding for 9 bits in our code for temperature resolution.
Lastly, we get a 0x02 in MOSI sent which corresponds to the address byte for the MSB register. This is followed by a MISO returned (in the second byte) of 0x19. In decimal, this hex value represents 25. This corresponds to the temperature reading of 25 degrees Celsius that was displayed on the web server. The integer part of the temperature is stored in the MSB register and the fractional part is stored in the LSB register. The LSB read earlier was 0x00, so there is no fractional part and the temperature is exactly 25 degrees Celsius.
The math also checks out: rawtemp = ((0x19 << 8) | 0x00) >> 4 = 0x1900 >> 4 = 0x0190 = 400, and 400 × 0.0625 = 25 degrees Celsius.

title: Lab 6: IoT, Web Server, and SPI
text:
Conclusion
The design successfully read temperature data from the DS1722 temperature sensor and displayed it on a web server. The user was able to control the LED and change the resolution of the temperature readings through the web interface. The SPI communication between the MCU and the temperature sensor was verified through logic traces, confirming that the correct data was being sent and received.
Additionally, the project demonstrated the integration of IoT concepts with embedded systems, showcasing how microcontrollers can interact with sensors and web servers to create interactive applications. The lab provided valuable hands-on experience in working with SPI communication, web server implementation, and real-time data processing.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
In this lab, we leveraged the MCU aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board, particularly the STM32L4xx model. With it, we can use the timer logic like a counter to trigger an output at a certain frequency. This is done via the TIM2 register built into the MCU, as well as by initializing the GPIO B pins to output a signal that powers a speaker at the desired frequency. With all these puzzle pieces, we can have the speaker play an array of notes and make a tune.
I spent approximately 14 hours on this lab altogether, including familiarizing myself with the idea and a whole lot of debugging.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
AI Prototype Summary






Figure 2: A screenshot of the AI’s response to the timer prompt.









NoteInitial Prompt Response






Timers to Use (220 Hz to 1 kHz)
The STM32L432KC includes several general-purpose and advanced timers suitable for signal and PWM generation:

TIM2 (32-bit): High-precision general-purpose timer. Its 32-bit width provides a massive counting range, making low frequencies easily reachable without risk of counter overflow.
TIM1 (16-bit): Advanced-control timer. Fully capable, but includes extra complex features (break inputs, dead-time) that are unnecessary for basic audio/PWM signals.
TIM15 & TIM16 (16-bit): General-purpose 16-bit timers. Suitable for basic signal output, though care must be taken to ensure the 16-bit limit (65,535) isn’t exceeded when selecting prescaler values.



Best Choice & Easy GPIO Pin Mapping
TIM2 Channel 1 mapping to PA0 (Pin A0 on the NUCLEO-L432KC board) is the best choice.

Why: TIM2 is a 32-bit timer, giving you maximum resolution for calculating duty cycles and frequencies.
Pin Connection: PA0 supports AF1 (Alternate Function 1) for TIM2_CH1. It breaks out cleanly on the outer headers of the Nucleo-32 board.



Relevant Formulas
Output frequency (\(f_{\text{PWM}}\)):
\[f_{\text{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\text{TIMCLK}}}{(\text{PSC} + 1) \times (\text{ARR} + 1)}\]

\(f_{\text{TIMCLK}}\): Timer input clock frequency (e.g., 80 MHz standard system clock).
\(\text{PSC}\): Prescaler register value (0 to 65,535).
\(\text{ARR}\): Auto-Reload Register value (defines the period).

Duty cycle (%):
\[\text{Duty Cycle} = \frac{\text{CCR1}}{\text{ARR} + 1} \times 100\%\]

\(\text{CCR1}\): Capture/Compare Register value (controls when the pin toggles).



Calculation Example (\(f_{\text{TIMCLK}} = 80\) MHz)
To maintain a high counter resolution, pick a fixed prescaler value. Set \(\text{PSC} = 79\) (divides the clock down to 1 MHz, or 1 µs per tick).
For 1000 Hz output:
\[\text{ARR} = \frac{80{,}000{,}000}{(79 + 1) \times 1000} - 1 = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{1000} - 1 = 999\]
For 220 Hz output:
\[\text{ARR} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{220} - 1 \approx 4544\]


Required Registers & Configuration Steps
To output a hardware PWM signal on pin PA0 without CPU overhead, configure the following registers:
Clock enable registers

RCC->AHB2ENR: Set bit GPIOAEN to enable the GPIOA clock.
RCC->APB1ENR1: Set bit TIM2EN to enable the TIM2 peripheral clock.

GPIO pin configuration (GPIOA)

GPIOA->MODER: Set MODER0 to 10 (Alternate Function Mode).
GPIOA->AFR[0]: Set AFSEL0 to 0001 (AF1) to select TIM2_CH1.

Timer configuration (TIM2)

TIM2->PSC: Set to 79 (1 MHz counter clock).
TIM2->ARR: Set to the desired frequency target (e.g., 999 for 1 kHz, 4544 for 220 Hz).
TIM2->CCR1: Set to half of ARR for a 50% square wave (e.g., 500 for 1 kHz).
TIM2->CCMR1: Set OC1M bits to 0110 (PWM Mode 1: active while CNT < CCR1), and set OC1PE to 1 (enable preload register).
TIM2->CCER: Set CC1E bit to 1 to enable output on Channel 1.
TIM2->CR1: Set CEN bit to 1 to enable the counter.





For clarity, the prompt was as follows:

What timers should I use on the STM32L432KC to generate frequencies ranging from 220Hz to 1kHz? What’s the best choice of timer if I want to easily connect it to a GPIO pin? What formulae are relevant, and what registers need to be set to configure them properly?

I prompted Gemini via the Harvey Mudd license (so my data would not be used to train the AI), and I was presented with the “Initial Prompt Response” block seen above. Notably, it is comprehensive and covers a lot about timer selection, along with some of the information I came across while reading the manual. The AI does conclude that TIM2 is ideal for practically the same reason I described: it is 32-bit. However, it opts for pin A0 because it supports Alternate Function 1. I instead went the route of using GPIO B and declaring it as a general purpose output, but I can see how PA0 also makes sense and may even be more effective, since it isn’t paired with an LED and AF1 seems well suited for this purpose. It also uses the same logic to enable the clock registers, but has to use GPIOA->MODER and declare that as Alternate Function mode. When I gave it the files, it functioned more as a table of contents with a summary, rather than pointing me to specific addresses and telling me what to do about those sections. I can see why that may be helpful, though.
Figure 2 shows a screenshot of the second prompting, and it seems pretty thorough as an overview if someone wanted to figure out where to go.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display
text:
In this lab, we built on the single seven segment display from Lab 1 and used the FPGA aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board to drive a dual seven segment display. Multiplexing logic selects which DIP switch input is shown on which digit and flashes the two hex digits fast enough that the flicker is undetectable to the human eye. The decoder and counter modules are identical to Lab 1; a new top-level module uses the parameterized counter to flash the digits and to select the right DIP switch and digit (i.e., the common anode of the dual seven segment display). Multiplexing lets us control two digits with just 9 pins. Using the counter module, we divide the internal 48 MHz clock by ~18’b0 (all ones, so the counter runs through its full 18-bit range), resulting in a clock of ~90 Hz (due to toggling), which is indeed sufficient.
This lab also included building a scanning module so a scanning signal is displayed at ~2 Hz on the internal LEDs when buttons on a keypad are pressed. The idea is that each row runs at a slightly different offset clock cycle, and pressing all 4 columns in conjunction results in a synchronized blinking. Furthermore, both designs took advantage of the physics of PNP and NPN transistors so the FPGA pins never drain more than 8 mA while still delivering sufficient current.
I spent approximately 15 hours on this lab altogether, including familiarizing myself with the idea and a whole lot of debugging.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display
Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated GitHub repository.

Block Diagram






Figure 1: Block diagram of the SystemVerilog design.



The block diagram in Figure 1 demonstrates the overall architecture of the design. The top-level module lab2_ea includes three submodules: the winker/counter (winker), which is parameterized to provide a range of frequencies to the top module or the scanner; the scanner (scanner), which cycles which bit of the [3:0] row output vector (fed into the keypad) is HIGH; and the 7-segment display logic module (decoder). Additionally, HSOSC is leveraged for an internal 48 MHz clock.


Schematic






Figure 2: Schematic of the physical circuit.



Figure 2 shows the electrical layout of the design. Because driving every segment at 10 mA is strenuous (especially if we consider a case where both digits display 8), 150 \(\Omega\) was the appropriate value per the equation \(R_{seg} = (3.3\,\text{V} - 2\,\text{V}) / 10\,\text{mA}\), making 150 \(\Omega\) our ideal choice.
The transistors and the resistor values associated with the keypad scanner were also paramount. First, the display was multiplexed by having two independent 2N3906 PNP transistors control the common anode of each digit (specifically, the collector pin of the transistor). These transistors are configured to saturate when the FPGA pin (connected to the base) reads LOW. The emitter is simply connected to +3.3 V.
Each of the four keypad rows uses an NPN setup. Following the E155 site instructions, the emitter is connected to the FPGA ground, and the base is connected to an FPGA pin (the row outputs) through a resistor (\(R_{base}\)). The collector is wired to the rows of the keypad as shown in Figure 2, and the columns are wired both to the FPGA as column inputs and to +3.3 V via a 1 k\(\Omega\) pull-up resistor. The value of this resistor is somewhat arbitrary and should just be a decent value for a pull-up. However, it does inform the value of \(R_{base}\). The equation is \(R_{base} = (3.3\,\text{V} - 0.7\,\text{V}) / I_{base}\), where 0.7 V is the base-emitter voltage drop and \(I_{base}\) is expected to be \(I_{collector}/10\), or 0.33 mA. This ultimately yields a value of 7.8 k\(\Omega\), though a 2.2 k\(\Omega\) resistor serves our purpose of saturating the transistor just fine.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, we leveraged the FPGA aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board (which was soldered and constructed per instructions on the E155 site). The FPGA was designed logically to illuminate two LEDs (also present on the Dev Board) following AND or XOR logic from a 4-input DIP switch. Second, a third LED on the Dev Board was instructed to blink at 2.4 Hz. This was done using a clock divider and the 48 MHz high speed oscillator on the board. Finally, the 4-input DIP switch was also logically connected to a 7-segment display such that the binary input would display the corresponding hexadecimal digit on the display. This lab took a total of 16 hours.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The first logic to approach was the 2 LEDs following simple gate logic. To do this, I used assign statements corresponding to the pins and the gate logic. For the testing methodology, a testbench was made and simulated that would confirm all possible outputs of the logic were properly observed and the LEDs illuminated as expected. This same testbench was also used to confirm module connections occurred and the on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was generating a clock signal at 48 MHz.






NoteSimple LED Gate Logic





assign led[0] = s[1] ^ s[0]; //XOR logic for one LED
assign led[1] = s[3] & s[2]; //AND logic for another LED



On the note of the high-speed oscillator, the int_osc signal generated by the top-level module was used as the clock input of a blinker submodule. With this input, a clock divider was created to convert 48 MHz to 2.4 Hz. This was done with a counter that reset when the counter reached 10,000,000. By parameterizing the MAX count, the same module can be simulated with a much smaller value. The module also includes “reset” and “en” inputs. After testing those with the proper LED output, we instantiate the module with a MAX count of 3 in the testbench. This allows us to see that when MAX count is reached, the counter does reset to 0 and the LED does toggle.






NoteBlinking Logic





logic [WIDTH-1:0] counter = 1'b0; //initial state of counter

// Simple clock divider
always_ff @(posedge int_osc)
    begin
        if (counter >= MAX) //We count to 10,000,000 because the LED toggles each time: 48 MHz / (2 x 10,000,000) = 2.4 Hz
            begin
            counter <= 0;
            fpga_blink_out <= ~fpga_blink_out;
            end
        else if (!reset)
            begin
                counter <= 0;
                fpga_blink_out <= 0;
            end
        else begin
            if (en) counter <= counter + 1;
        end
    end



Finally, the design logic for the seven segment display was implemented using an always_comb block with cases covering every 4-bit binary input and lighting up the relevant segments to create the hexadecimal digit. The seven bit output simply follows the A-G segments as defined in the E155 logic to toggle segments. To test this, I covered all 16 cases and asserted the logical outputs and it passed with flying colors! (get it?)






NoteSeven Segment Combinational Logic





always_comb
    begin
        case(s)
            4'b0000: seg = 7'b0000001; //0
            4'b0001: seg = 7'b1001111; //1
            4'b0010: seg = 7'b0010010; //2
            4'b0011: seg = 7'b0000110; //3
            4'b0100: seg = 7'b1001100; //4
            4'b0101: seg = 7'b0100100; //5
            4'b0110: seg = 7'b0100000; //6
            4'b0111: seg = 7'b0001111; //7
            4'b1000: seg = 7'b0000000; //8
            4'b1001: seg = 7'b0000100; //9
            4'b1010: seg = 7'b0001000; //A
            4'b1011: seg = 7'b1100000; //B
            4'b1100: seg = 7'b0110001; //C
            4'b1101: seg = 7'b1000010; //D
            4'b1110: seg = 7'b0110000; //E
            4'b1111: seg = 7'b0111000; //F
            default: seg = 7'b1111111; //default case
        endcase
    end

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
With a few edits to the hardware from Lab 2, we can use the multiplexed display logic and row scanning on the keypad to reliably receive inputs from the keypad and show them on the display. Specifically, this lab aims to provide functionality to the keypad such that the display records the last two buttons hit on the keypad. To achieve this, a finite state machine (FSM) reading the inputs (to handle presses, lack of press, and multiple presses) was used in tandem with a register that shifts the last digit to the second display. Naturally, other modules are required to handle synchronization and debouncing on the keypad. This lab was immensely thought-provoking and required clever manipulation of, and communication between, modules.
I spent approximately 18 hours (so far) on this lab altogether, including familiarizing myself with the idea, debugging, and revising.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated GitHub repository.

Block Diagram






Figure 1: Block diagram of the SystemVerilog design.



The block diagram in Figure 1 demonstrates the overall architecture of the design. The top-level module lab2_ea includes three submodules: the winker/counter (winker), which is parameterized to provide a range of frequencies to the top module or the scanner; the scanner (scanner), which cycles which bit of the [3:0] row output vector (fed into the keypad) is HIGH; and the 7-segment display logic module (decoder). Additionally, HSOSC is leveraged for an internal 48 MHz clock.


Schematic






Figure 2: Schematic of the physical circuit.



Figure 2 shows the electrical layout of the design. Because driving every segment at 10 mA is strenuous (especially if we consider a case where both digits display 8), 150 \(\Omega\) was the appropriate value per the equation \(R_{seg} = (3.3\,\text{V} - 2\,\text{V}) / 10\,\text{mA}\), making 150 \(\Omega\) our ideal choice.
The transistors and the resistor values associated with the keypad scanner were also paramount. First, the display was multiplexed by having two independent 2N3906 PNP transistors control the common anode of each digit (specifically, the collector pin of the transistor). These transistors are configured to saturate when the FPGA pin (connected to the base) reads LOW. The emitter is simply connected to +3.3 V.
Each of the four keypad rows uses an NPN setup. Following the E155 site instructions, the emitter is connected to the FPGA ground, and the base is connected to an FPGA pin (the row outputs) through a resistor (\(R_{base}\)). The collector is wired to the rows of the keypad as shown in Figure 2, and the columns are wired both to the FPGA as column inputs and to +3.3 V via a 1 k\(\Omega\) pull-up resistor. The value of this resistor is somewhat arbitrary and should just be a decent value for a pull-up. However, it does inform the value of \(R_{base}\). The equation is \(R_{base} = (3.3\,\text{V} - 0.7\,\text{V}) / I_{base}\), where 0.7 V is the base-emitter voltage drop and \(I_{base}\) is expected to be \(I_{collector}/10\), or 0.33 mA. This ultimately yields a value of 7.8 k\(\Omega\), though a 2.2 k\(\Omega\) resistor serves our purpose of saturating the transistor just fine.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
In this lab, we once again leveraged the MCU aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board, particularly the STM32L4xx model. The idea was to use interrupts to read a quadrature encoder and measure the speed in rev/s (and by extension RPM) and direction of a 25GA-370 motor spinning in either direction. Reading the encoder with interrupts lets us check that the encoder functions properly and that no pulses are skipped, since the printed speed and the direction logic (CW or CCW) would otherwise glitch. With all of these puzzle pieces, we are able to decode the motor’s encoder and assess the use of interrupts against other strategies like polling. The interrupts worked: we know no pulses were skipped, because skipped pulses made the readings randomly switch direction even when no hardware was changed. That was a problem earlier, but it was quickly patched.
I spent approximately 18 hours on this lab altogether, including familiarizing myself with the idea and a whole lot of debugging.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
Using SEGGER Embedded Studio, the logic of this lab was contained in a header file and a main file.
There are many timers onboard the MCU but TIM2 has 32 bits and is generally recommended so overflow doesn’t occur and we can leverage its interrupt as long as we use pins PA1 and PA2, which also feature IRQ handlers. These are also great because the MCU datasheet states in section 4 Table 14 that these have an I/O Structure of FT_a which is 5V tolerant.
First, data being read out regarding the bits of calculation and the RPS require 1 kHz refresh in the terminal and computing as specified. Since TIM2 was selected, this is 1 ms and with an IRQHandler we can make it so that when ARR (aka SAMPL, aka sampling frequency) reaches 999 (and we add 1 in the calculations), it triggers an interrupt. This corresponds with 1 second, which is what we want. It should even be compatible with the EXTI IRQ handlers.
The code also notes PPR and is editable to be configured with a motor operating at 150 RPM (408 PPR) though this can be changed. Accounting for the 2 interrupts and the rising and falling edges, we don’t just double this. This was an issue that has been fixed, and it is now an estimated 1632 counts per revolution.
With all this in mind, to calculate RPS, the formula is RPS = count / (cntsperrev*(SAMPL+1) / 1000). We take into account the timer duration (for that PS of RPS) as well as the expected counts per revolution and count which corresponds to observed pulses in both pins (and rising/falling edges).
Now, an important question to ask is why the need for interrupts. Why would interrupts be better than polling or timers?
Implementing polling would theoretically be far easier than interrupts where we simply read the encoder values as prev, do the calculation and we can do a check to do a calculation every time. Polling IS simple to integrate, but it works by counting how many times it reads a value in that 1 second interval. By only relying on digitalRead and timers, we read a value and there is a delay/wait time when a pulse is read. If we’re lucky, it’s fine, but there is a high risk to skip a pulse and be off loop resulting in wildly wrong values or changes in direction where there shouldn’t be. Even if we have a high sampling frequency and low computation, there will still be enough inconsistency for the risk of skipping a pulse to be nonzero.
This also brings up concerns with sampling as a whole with polling and how some speeds can’t be recorded if sampling frequency is not twice or more as the RPS.
Interrupts, theoretically, resolve this because it is not doing the computation all the time and waiting. We only run the computational code when we read something worth processing to trigger an interrupt and thus, processing is more fluid.
In other words, polling has you trapped in a “Data?” while(1) loop which consumes 100% of the CPU’s processing power just for checking. It depends on that loop length for execution and moving on, and it is beholden to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.
When implemented, we see the theoretical limitations. For polling, even if we use 80 MHz clock (max for the MCU), our cycles are 12.5 ns and in that time, we have to read the IDR, mask the bit, compare, and then go back in basic assembly. Even with severe optimization, it’s 80 MHz divided by let’s say 5 cycles to do this all. That’s 16 million polls. In reality, with the printf() and register saving that number goes considerably down. We get an approximate (from experimentation) of 30-50 kHz which is not great.
The limit for an interrupt is latency and the ISR because the NVIC can handle multiple interrupts and neither affects each other. Latency isn’t a concerning issue but the ISR execution time is how much time is spent in the IRQ handlers. If it takes 100 clock cycles (based on the code below, that’s more than reasonable), then our limit is 80 MHz/(12+100) or 714 kHz. That is FAR better even in the worst case scenario.

title: AUV Sensor Deployment & Telemetry System
text:
Course: E80 Experimental Engineering, Harvey Mudd College (Team 37, Section 3)
Team: Eduardo Ambriz Lazo, Lily Anfang, Nicholas Dass, Quinn Miyamoto
Timeline: January – May 2025 · deployed at Baby Beach, Dana Point, CA
Tools: Teensy 4.0 Arduino MATLAB FSR 400 HC-SR04 AH9246 hall sensor 555 timer Op-amps Machining
Full report: Evaluating the Accuracy of Ultrasonic Waves and Force for Determining Distance (PDF)

title: AUV Sensor Deployment & Telemetry System
text:
Overview
For our final E80 project, my team built an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) that was supposed to measure the distance to an object it was following. Ideally, that distance would feed a control loop on the motor PWM so the vehicle could hold a constant following distance.
Instead of relying on a single sensor, we compared two very different ways of measuring distance:

Ultrasonic time of flight with an HC-SR04, which sends out pulses and times the echo.
Force and Hooke’s Law, where a force-sensing resistor (FSR) reads the force on a spring-loaded extrusion and a calibrated spring constant turns that force into a distance.

We also built an anemometer around a hall effect sensor to log wind speed during deployment, so we could explain any odd behavior in the distance data.
Then it rained at Dana Point. The ultrasonic sensor was not waterproof and failed, so the deployment turned into a test of the novel FSR-and-spring approach to object detection.

text:

title: AUV Sensor Deployment & Telemetry System
text:
The Sensors

Force-Sensing Resistor and Spring
The idea comes straight from Hooke’s Law, \(F_s = k\,\Delta x\), so \(\Delta x = F_s / k\). If the FSR measures the force on a spring with a known spring constant \(k\), the spring’s compression tells us how far away an object is when the extrusion touches it. FSRs are normally used to detect pressure, so using one this way was a creative twist, and FSRs are also easy to calibrate with just a few known loads.
The FSR sits in a voltage divider with a 10 kΩ resistor:
\[V_{out} = \frac{R_g}{R_g + R_{p1}} V_{in}\]
An op-amp stage then adds gain and an offset so the signal lands in a 1–3 V range, comfortably inside the Teensy’s readable range.






Figure 1: Circuit for the FSR: voltage divider followed by a gain and offset stage built from OP07 op-amps.



We calibrated the sensor by applying known forces and measuring the output. A cubic polynomial fit the force-to-resistance relationship very well (R² = 0.999), and the force-to-voltage relationship through our actual circuit also fit a cubic (R² = 0.989), which is the one we used.









Figure 2: Force vs. resistance calibration (R² = 0.999).











Figure 3: Force vs. voltage calibration through the circuit (R² = 0.989).






The last calibration was the spring itself, which relates the sensed force (and so the voltage) to a physical displacement. Running multiple trials gave an uncertainty on each distance value.






Figure 4: Spring calibration curve (R² = 0.988), with uncertainty bars.

Ultrasonic Distance Sensor
The HC-SR04 estimates distance from how long an ultrasonic pulse takes to bounce back: distance = (high-level time × 340 m/s) / 2. It needs a trigger pulse, so the circuit uses an NA555P timer in astable configuration that fires the trigger roughly every 345 ms. The sensor’s echo output is then scaled with a non-inverting op-amp stage (gain of 4), so about 1 meter of range maps to 0–2.1 V.






Figure 5: Ultrasonic sensor circuit: 555 timer trigger on the left, op-amp scaling stage on the right.



We calibrated it by recording the average peak voltage over 10 trials at 10 cm increments from 10 cm to 1 m. A straight line fit well (R² = 0.993), with distance in cm ≈ 46.5 × V − 3.01.









Figure 6: Ultrasonic calibration curve (R² = 0.993).











Figure 7: Oscilloscope trace of the echo output in a dry test.






A dry test on the AUV’s protoboard showed the setup only reached about 1.2 m, well short of the 4 m the datasheet promises.


Hall Effect Anemometer
To log the weather, we built a cup anemometer that carries a magnet. Each time the magnet passes the AH9246 hall effect sensor, the output drops, and counting those drops gives revolutions per second. A single OP07 op-amp conditions the output to 1–3 V.






Figure 8: Hall effect sensor circuit with a single OP07 op-amp.



The software side took the most work. We extended the base ADC loop so it watches for voltage drops, counts revolutions with an interrupt, and computes RPS over each 69 ms sampling window. Calibration happened in a wind tunnel in two steps: first relating the tunnel’s fan RPM to wind speed, then relating the anemometer’s RPS to that wind speed.









Figure 9: Wind tunnel fan RPM vs. wind speed.











Figure 10: Anemometer RPS vs. wind speed (R² = 0.886).

title: AUV Sensor Deployment & Telemetry System
text:
Mechanical Design
The frame had a lot of competing requirements. The motors had to be underwater, the anemometer had to be elevated to catch real wind, and the electronics box had to stay dry above the waterline.

Stability: a large surface area keeps the AUV from tipping, but adds weight up high. We kept the center of mass below the center of buoyancy so the vehicle self-rights, and added pool noodles for flotation.
Dry electronics: the box holding the Teensy, motherboard, and protoboard sits above the water for safety.
Anemometer frame: the cups spin a magnet past the hall sensor. Mounting that assembly tilted the vehicle’s balance, which is why the other two sensors got their own second frame.
Spring and extrusion frame: a CAD-designed housing holds a spring-loaded extrusion about 14.5 inches long that changes length as force is applied, and an elevated panel gives the ultrasonic sensor something to reflect off.










Figure 11: Sketches of the overall mechanical assembly (side, isometric, and top views).











Figure 12: Cutaway of the anemometer showing the magnet and the hall effect sensor.












Figure 13: CAD model of the ultrasonic sensor frame and the spring-and-arm assembly that triggers the FSR.

title: AUV Sensor Deployment & Telemetry System
AUV Sensor Deployment & Telemetry System
text:
Results

Ultrasonic sensor: no usable data. Despite repeated attempts to trigger it with a panel in close proximity, its output stayed constant after the rain damage.
Anemometer: worked as expected. Live readings ranged from about 2 m/s to 6.21 m/s, in line with the day’s reported average wind of 14 mph (about 6.25 m/s). The remaining discrepancy was likely due to the anemometer’s low elevation.
FSR and spring: the main result. Within the pre-specified distance during deployment, the FSR output swung between 1 and 3 V for forces of roughly 0.36 N, 0.853 N, and 1.36 N, which supports the force-to-distance idea.

We compared two trials with different motor power: Deployment 1 at 120 PWM and Deployment 2 at 290 PWM.









Figure 15: Deployment 1 raw data at 120 PWM (anemometer on top, FSR below).











Figure 16: Deployment 2 raw data at 290 PWM.






In Deployment 1, the FSR looked nearly digital instead of showing the slow rise in force our dry tests produced. Comparing against the video showed the FSR’s response was valid, but the gradual change was missing from the data. The most likely cause is aliasing: at a 14.4 Hz sampling rate, the force can change faster than we sample it.

title: AUV Sensor Deployment & Telemetry System
text:
What I’d Do Differently

Waterproof the ultrasonic sensor and rework its output into an analog voltage proportional to distance, so it can drive a real control loop on motor PWM, the same way the anemometer software works.
Raise the sampling rate to avoid aliasing and make post-processing easier.
Elevate the anemometer more so it sees real wind speeds.
Recalibrate any replacement sensors before deployment.

This project showed how much each sensor demands in its own way: mechanical design for the spring and frame, software for the anemometer, and careful circuit work for the ultrasonic sensor.

Overview

title: RISC-V Multi-Cycle Processor & FPGA Synthesizer
text:
The Processor
In a multi-cycle design, each instruction takes several clock cycles, and a finite state machine (FSM) sequences the shared datapath through those steps.

Defined a custom ISA.
Designed the datapath components: the ALU, registers, and memory.
Implemented the FSM that controls multi-cycle instruction execution.
